opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing for us has always been to stay small and very dense in terms of talent. When we started Mistral, the founding team was just a handful of people, and we trained our first models with a very small group. That was a deliberate choice, not just a constraint. In research, adding more people doesn't make things go faster linearly. Past a certain point, you spend more time coordinating, aligning, and syncing than actually running experiments.

So when we hire, we're very selective. We look for people who are strong on both the science and the engineering side, because in this field you can't really separate the two anymore. The person who has the idea for a new data mixture or a training trick should also be able to implement it, launch the job on the cluster, debug it when it breaks at 3 a.m., and analyze the results. That kind of profile is rare, so we'd rather wait to find the right person than grow fast just to grow.

Of course, as the company grows, we're doing more things: pretraining, post-training, multimodal, code, reasoning, and also a lot of work with customers. So the team does need to grow. But we try to keep a structure where each team is small, owns a clear piece of the problem, and has a lot of autonomy. Small teams with a lot of compute and a lot of trust tend to move much faster than big teams with a lot of process.

It's also about culture. When the team is small, everyone knows what everyone else is working on, people share results very openly, and bad ideas get killed quickly. That's something we really want to preserve, even as we scale. The bottleneck isn't really headcount. It's compute, data, and having people with good intuition about what's worth trying.

r001.rationale: The response says Mistral deliberately keeps teams small because adding people increases coordination, while small autonomous teams move faster.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that we try very hard not to grow the science team as fast as we could. When we started, the whole company was a handful of people in a room, and the thing that struck all of us coming from Meta and DeepMind was how much faster things moved when there were ten of you and no coordination overhead. At a big lab, you'd spend half your week in meetings about which team owns which part of the pipeline. Here, if you want to try something on the data mix, you just do it, and by the evening you have a result.

So when we hire, the question I ask is not "do we have enough people," it's "will this person make the people already here faster or slower." Pretraining in particular is a game where a very small number of people make almost all the important decisions: the data, the architecture choices, the hyperparameters, how you run the scaling experiments. You cannot really parallelize those decisions across fifty people. If you try, you get a committee, and committees train bad models.

Where we do scale is on the things that are genuinely parallel. Data curation for different languages, evaluation, post-training, infrastructure, inference optimization. Those benefit from more hands. So the shape of the team ends up being a small core on pretraining that we protect quite jealously, and then wider rings around it that grow as the product and the model surface grows.

The other thing is that we are compute-constrained much more than we are people-constrained. Adding a researcher doesn't give them more GPUs to run experiments on. If anything, it splits the cluster further. So there's a natural ceiling where another hire just means everyone waits longer for their jobs to run. We'd rather have a smaller team with enough compute per person to actually test their ideas than a large team that spends its time queued.

And honestly, I think the big labs got the size wrong, and that was part of the opportunity. The results that matter in this field in the last few years mostly came from groups of ten or twenty people, even inside organizations of thousands. We just wanted to build the company around that fact rather than against it.

r001.rationale: The response says Mistral deliberately limits science-team growth because small teams move faster and avoid coordination overhead.

astra-6.text: I think we want to keep the science team relatively small. There’s a lot of value in having everyone understand what everyone else is working on, and being able to exchange ideas very quickly. As you grow, you can do more things in parallel, but you also introduce more coordination overhead. So we’re not trying to maximize the number of researchers. We want to hire very strong people who can work independently and bring something complementary to the team, and grow at a pace where we preserve that way of working.

sol-6.1.text: I think we want to keep the science team relatively small. The goal is not to hire as many researchers as possible, but to have a very high density of talent, with people who can work independently and also collaborate very closely. When the team gets bigger, you spend more time coordinating, and it becomes harder for everyone to understand what everyone else is doing. So we are hiring, but we want to be careful and make sure each person really adds something to the team.
